title: What a Petition Is and Is Not
body:
A petition is a written request, signed by supporters, asking a decision-maker, such as a council, a legislature, or an organization, to take a specific action. Petitions work because they show, in a countable and checkable form, how many people support an ask, and because many decision-making bodies have formal rules for receiving and responding to them. A petition is not a vote, and it does not by itself force a decision: its power depends on the rules that govern it, which differ sharply by jurisdiction and by body, and on the quality of its signatures, which must usually be verified before they count. A petition is also not a protest, a survey, or a mailing list, although it may accompany any of those, and confusing it with them leads to petitions that are counted poorly or not at all. This record explains the petition itself; organizing a campaign around one is covered by the companion organizing basics database, cross-linked from here.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part petition definition check run before drafting. First, name the decision-maker the petition addresses, because a petition addressed to nobody in particular cannot be received or answered. Second, name the specific action requested, in one sentence, because vague asks cannot be verified or acted on. Third, check the receiving body's petition rules, including any form, threshold, and deadline, before collecting a single signature. Fourth, decide how signatures will be collected and verified, because a petition built on unverifiable signatures will fail at the validation stage however strong its support. The demo below sorts three example asks by whether they are specific enough to petition on, which is the sorting a drafter does first.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for what a petition is and is not. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 'repair the library roof' -> specific; 'make things better' -> too vague; 'extend library hours to 8pm' -> specific; specific asks: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when starting any petition, and in civic education. Do not use it as legal advice about petition rights or procedures in any jurisdiction, because rules differ and this record is educational reference only. Do not use it to claim a petition guarantees an outcome, because most petition systems guarantee consideration or a response, not the action requested. title: Writing a Clear Petition Ask
body:
A clear petition ask is the most important sentence in the petition, because every signature endorses it, every validator checks against it, and every decision-maker responds to it. A good ask names the decision-maker, the action, and the scope in one sentence, such as asking a named council to repair a named facility by a named date, and it avoids vague language, multiple unrelated actions, and demands that the decision-maker has no power to grant. The ask should also be honest about what it seeks: a request for consideration, a request for a named action, and a request for a change in law are different asks with different consequences, and supporters should know which one they are signing. Drafting the ask first, and testing it on people unfamiliar with the issue, catches most drafting errors before signatures are collected, when fixing them is cheap.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part ask draft. First, write the ask in one sentence, naming decision-maker, action, and scope. Second, check that the decision-maker actually has the power to grant it, because an ask addressed to the wrong body will be rejected however many sign it. Third, remove every second action, so the petition asks one thing, because multi-action petitions split support and complicate responses. Fourth, test the sentence on three people unfamiliar with the issue, and rewrite anything they misunderstand. Fifth, freeze the wording before collecting signatures, because changing the ask mid-collection can invalidate earlier signatures under some rules. The demo below checks three draft asks against the one-sentence and one-action tests, which is the check a drafter runs first.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for writing a clear petition ask. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: council repairs library roof -> passes; council fixes everything -> fails one-ask test; council extends hours and repairs roof -> fails one-ask test; passing drafts: 1 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when drafting any petition, and in civic education. Do not use it as legal advice about what a particular body can or must do, because powers differ by jurisdiction and body. Do not use it to draft an ask that misleads supporters about its effect, because a petition's legitimacy depends on supporters knowing what they signed. title: Petition Wording That Holds Up
body:
Petition wording holds up when it is factual, neutral in tone, and precise about what supporters endorse, because wording that overstates, misleads, or attacks individuals invites rejection, dispute, and distrust. The background statement that accompanies a petition should state facts that can be checked, cite sources where claims are made, and separate facts from opinions, so a reader can tell what is established, what is argued, and what is asked. Wording should avoid claims about named individuals that cannot be substantiated, because defamatory statements in a petition can create legal risk for its organizers and undermine the petition itself, and it should avoid language that misstates the decision-maker's powers or the petition's effect. A petition that reads as careful and checkable is more likely to be received, verified, and answered seriously, whatever the decision-maker's view of its ask.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part wording check. First, underline every factual claim in the background statement and ask whether it can be checked from a named source, removing or sourcing anything that cannot. Second, separate facts from opinions visibly, so supporters sign the ask knowing which parts are argument. Third, remove any statement about a named individual that cannot be substantiated, and any claim about the petition's effect that overstates what the rules guarantee. Fourth, read the whole petition as a stranger would, and rewrite anything that could be read as promising an outcome the petition cannot deliver. The demo below screens three background claims by whether they are sourced, which is the screen a drafter runs before publishing.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for petition wording that holds up. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record when drafting or reviewing petition wording, and in civic education. Do not use it as legal advice about defamation or petition law, which differ by jurisdiction; organizers facing a risky claim should seek qualified advice. Do not use it to sanitize a petition into vagueness, because precision and honesty strengthen a petition, while vagueness weakens it. title: Who Can Sign: Eligibility Basics
body:
Who can sign a petition depends on the petition's rules, and collecting signatures from people who cannot validly sign them is the most common way a petition loses count. Some petitions are open to anyone who supports the ask, including people outside the area. Others, especially formal petitions to a council or legislature, require signers to be residents, voters, or members of a defined group, and to meet age or registration conditions. Some require a full name and address, some require a signature matching a register, and some allow electronic signatures under specific conditions. The organizer's job is to learn the eligibility rules for their specific petition before collecting anything, to state them plainly on the petition itself, and to collect only signatures that meet them, because ineligible signatures do not merely fail to count: under some systems they can delay validation or cast doubt on the whole petition.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part eligibility check. First, read the receiving body's petition rules and extract the eligibility conditions in plain words: who, where, and what proof. Second, write those conditions on the petition form itself, in the same plain words, so signers can self-check before signing. Third, train every collector to ask the eligibility question before accepting a signature, rather than collecting first and checking later. Fourth, keep a separate count of signatures collected and signatures believed eligible, so the organizer knows the petition's real strength before submission. The demo below sorts a small set of would-be signers by eligibility under an example residents-only rule, which is the sorting collectors must do in practice.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for who can sign: eligibility basics. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: resident, adult -> eligible; visitor, adult -> not eligible under residents-only rule; resident, under age -> not eligible under residents-only rule; resident, adult -> eligible; eligible signatures: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when planning any petition collection, and in civic education. Do not use it as a statement of the rules for any particular petition, because eligibility rules differ by body and jurisdiction, and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to collect personal data beyond what the rules require, because signer privacy matters, and excess data creates risk without adding count. title: Paper Petitions: Collecting Signatures
body:
Paper petitions remain common, and their strength is also their weakness: a paper form is easy to sign anywhere, but every signature must be legible, complete, and verifiable, or it will not count. A good paper form carries the ask at the top of every page, not only the first, so no signature is ever collected on a page whose ask the signer did not see; it carries the eligibility conditions in plain words; it provides one row per signer, with the fields the rules require, such as printed name, signature, and address or ward; and it leaves no room for ambiguity, such as shared rows, overwritten entries, or signatures without printed names. Collectors should check each form as it is completed, while the signer is present and can correct it, rather than discovering illegible entries weeks later when correction is impossible.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part paper collection routine. First, prepare forms with the ask on every page and the eligibility conditions printed on them. Second, brief collectors on the eligibility question, the required fields, and the rule that no row is ever pre-filled or signed on someone else's behalf. Third, check each completed row at the point of collection, for legibility, completeness, and eligibility, and correct it with the signer present. Fourth, number and store completed pages securely, in order, so no page is lost, duplicated, or mixed with another petition's pages. Fifth, count pages and rows as collection proceeds, keeping the running eligible estimate separate from the raw count. The demo below checks a small batch of paper rows for completeness, which is the check collectors run on the spot.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for paper petitions: collecting signatures. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: name + signature + address -> complete; signature only -> incomplete - correct with signer present; name + signature, no address -> incomplete - correct with signer present; name + signature + address -> complete; complete rows: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record for any paper petition collection, and in collector training. Do not use it to accept signatures on someone else's behalf, to pre-fill rows, or to alter entries after signing, because each of those can invalidate signatures and damage the petition's credibility. Do not use it to collect more personal data than the rules require. title: Online Petitions: Platforms and Pitfalls
body:
Online petitions reach supporters quickly, but they carry pitfalls that paper petitions do not, and organizers who ignore them may collect thousands of signatures that no receiving body will count. The first pitfall is platform choice: a petition hosted on a general campaign platform may not satisfy a formal body's rules, which may require its own portal, its own form, or its own verification method, so a platform petition and a formal petition are different things, and the organizer must know which one they are running. The second pitfall is verification: online signatures are easier to fake, duplicate, or collect from ineligible signers, so formal systems check them more strictly, and a petition with many unverifiable signatures may be discounted heavily. The third pitfall is data: online platforms collect signer data under their own terms, and organizers must understand what data is collected, who holds it, and what signers consented to, before inviting people to sign.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part online petition check. First, confirm whether the receiving body accepts the chosen platform's signatures, or requires its own portal, before launching. Second, design the online form to collect exactly the fields the rules require, with eligibility stated plainly and a check against duplicates. Third, monitor signatures as they arrive for duplicates, ineligible entries, and suspicious patterns, and remove or flag them promptly rather than presenting an inflated count. Fourth, state the data handling plainly to signers: what is collected, who holds it, and whether signers will be contacted afterwards, and honor that statement. The demo below screens a small batch of online signatures for duplicates, which is the screen organizers run continuously.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for online petitions: platforms and pitfalls. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record when planning any online petition, and in civic education. Do not use it as a recommendation of any platform, because no vendor is named or endorsed here, and platform terms change. title: Signature Validation: How Signatures Are Checked
body:
Signature validation is the process by which a receiving body checks that a petition's signatures are real, eligible, and countable, and it is the stage where many petitions lose a large share of their count. Validation typically checks several things: that each signature is accompanied by the required fields, that the signer meets the eligibility conditions, that the signature is not a duplicate of another signature on the same petition, that the signature is genuine rather than forged or entered on someone else's behalf, and, for formal petitions, that the signer appears on the relevant register where one is used. Some bodies validate every signature; others validate a sample and project the result, rejecting the petition if the projected valid count falls below a threshold. Organizers who understand validation collect differently: they check eligibility and completeness at collection, they avoid duplicates, and they collect a margin above any threshold, because some loss at validation is normal and expected.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-part validation-ready routine. First, collect a margin above the threshold, because validation loss is normal, and the margin is planned, not hoped for. Second, check completeness and eligibility at collection, while correction is still possible. Third, deduplicate continuously, across collectors and pages, because duplicates found by validators count against credibility as well as count. Fourth, keep the petition's pages and records in order, so validators can trace any signature to its page and its collector. Fifth, expect the validation result to be lower than the raw count, and plan the submission message around the verified count, not the raw one. The demo below applies a small validation screen to a batch and counts the survivors, which is the arithmetic organizers should do before submission.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature validation: how signatures are checked. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: raw count: 5; valid count: 2; validation loss: 3 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when planning and running any petition, and in civic education. Do not use it as a statement of any particular body's validation method, because methods differ, and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to dispute a validation result without evidence, because disputes need specific, checkable claims about specific signatures, not general disagreement with the outcome. title: Invalid Signatures: Common Reasons
body:
Signatures are most often invalidated for ordinary, preventable reasons, not for fraud, and knowing the common reasons is the best protection against them. The most common reasons are incompleteness, such as a missing printed name, address, or signature where the rules require it; illegibility, where the name or address cannot be read; ineligibility, where the signer does not meet the petition's conditions, such as residence or age; duplication, where the same person signs twice, whether by mistake or design; and mismatch, where the signature or details do not match the register or record the validator checks against. Less common but more serious are signatures entered on someone else's behalf, which may be treated as forgery and can damage the whole petition's credibility. Each reason has a prevention: completeness and legibility are checked at collection, eligibility is asked before signing, duplicates are screened continuously, and no signature is ever entered for another person.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-reason prevention checklist used in collector training and in pre-submission review. First, completeness: every row carries every required field. Second, legibility: every name and address can be read by a stranger, not only by the collector. Third, eligibility: every signer was asked the eligibility question before signing. Fourth, duplication: the batch has been screened across all pages and collectors. Fifth, authenticity: every signature was made by the signer named, in person or through the authorized electronic method, and no row was altered after signing. The demo below classifies a small batch by invalidity reason, which is the classification organizers use to fix their collection before submission.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for invalid signatures: common reasons. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: incomplete: 2; illegible: 1; ineligible: 1; duplicate: 2; valid: 14; total rows: 20 valid: 14 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record in collector training and pre-submission review. Do not use it to alter entries after signing in order to fix them, because alteration after signing can itself invalidate a signature and damage credibility; the remedy is to re-collect correctly. Do not use it to accuse any signer of fraud on the basis of a classification alone, because most invalidity is error, not dishonesty. title: Circulating: Places, Permissions, and Conduct
body:
Circulating a petition means taking it to the people who may sign it, and the places, permissions, and conduct of circulation matter as much as the petition's wording. Public places, private premises, workplaces, schools, and online spaces each have different rules about whether petitioning is allowed, who must give permission, and what conduct is acceptable, and organizers who ignore those rules risk removal, complaints, or signatures collected in circumstances a validator may question. Good circulation conduct is consistent everywhere: collectors identify themselves and the petition honestly, they state the ask and the eligibility conditions plainly, they never pressure, mislead, or pay for signatures unless the rules explicitly allow it, they never sign on anyone's behalf, and they leave a place when asked, because a petition collected through pressure or deception loses legitimacy even where its signatures are technically valid.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part circulation plan. First, list the circulation places and, for each, confirm whether permission is needed and from whom, before collecting there. Second, brief collectors on the conduct rules: honest identification, plain statement of ask and eligibility, no pressure, no misleading claims, no signing for others, and no payment unless explicitly permitted. Third, equip collectors with the petition, the eligibility wording, and a contact for questions, so no collector improvises rules on the spot. Fourth, keep a circulation log: where, when, and by whom each batch was collected, so any question about a batch can be answered from the log. The demo below lists a small circulation plan by permission status, which is the plan organizers complete before their first collection day.

title: Counting and Presenting Signatures
body:
Counting and presenting signatures is where a petition's credibility is made or lost, because decision-makers and the public judge a petition by whether its numbers are honest, checkable, and clearly stated. An honest count distinguishes three numbers and never merges them: the raw count, which is every signature collected; the estimated valid count, which is the raw count minus duplicates, ineligible, and incomplete entries found by the organizer's own screening; and the verified count, which is the count the receiving body confirms after validation, and which is the only count that formally matters. Presenting the raw count as the petition's strength, without the screening that produced the estimated valid count, misleads supporters and decision-makers alike, and the gap between a claimed count and a verified count is remembered long after the petition itself. A petition presented with all three numbers, and with its method stated, is trusted even when its verified count is lower than hoped.

Method. The working method for this record is a three-number count and presentation routine. First, count raw signatures by page and by collector, and reconcile the page totals to the grand total, so no page is double-counted or lost. Second, screen for duplicates, ineligibility, and incompleteness, and record the estimated valid count with the reasons for each deduction. Third, present the petition with all three numbers where the rules allow, stating the screening method plainly, and use the verified count, once known, as the petition's public figure. The demo below reconciles a small count across pages and computes the estimated valid count, which is the arithmetic every organizer does before submission.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for counting and presenting signatures. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: raw count: 60; deductions (duplicates, ineligible, incomplete): 7; estimated valid count: 53 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record in petition planning, collection management, and submission. Do not use it to inflate a count by any means, including counting duplicates, ineligible signatures, or signatures from another petition, because inflation destroys the credibility the petition needs. Do not use it to hide the screening method, because a count without a method cannot be trusted. title: Submitting a Petition: Steps and Receipts
body:
Submitting a petition is a formal step with its own rules, and petitions have failed at submission for reasons that have nothing to do with support: the wrong form, the wrong office, a missed deadline, a missing cover sheet, or no proof that submission happened. A good submission routine starts before collection ends: the organizer confirms the receiving office, the required form and format, the deadline and how it is counted, the cover information required, such as the organizer's contact and the petition's ask, and the method of submission, whether in person, by post, or through a portal, with its own proof requirements. On submission day, the organizer delivers the petition as the rules require, obtains a receipt or acknowledgment naming the petition, the count submitted, and the date, and keeps a complete copy of everything submitted, because the copy is the organizer's protection if the original is questioned, lost, or disputed.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-step submission routine. First, confirm the office, form, format, deadline, and cover requirements in writing from the receiving body, well before the deadline. Second, assemble the petition in the required order, with pages numbered and counted, and the three-number count prepared. Third, make a complete copy of the submission, page by page, and store it securely. Fourth, submit by the required method and obtain a receipt or acknowledgment naming the petition, the count, and the date, following up if none arrives within the body's stated time. Fifth, record the submission in the petition's log and inform signers and supporters that submission has happened, with the submitted count stated honestly. The demo below checks a small submission checklist, which is the checklist organizers run on submission day.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: submission ready: 3 of 5 steps; still to do: ['copy kept', 'receipt obtained'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when planning and carrying out any petition submission. Do not use it as a statement of any particular body's submission rules, because rules differ, and the receiving body's current rules govern. Do not use it to submit after a deadline in the hope of leniency, because deadlines in formal petition systems are often strict, and late submission may mean the petition is not received at all. title: Jurisdiction Variation: Local, Regional, National
body:
Petition rules vary sharply by jurisdiction and by level, and a petition method that works in one place may fail in another, which is why jurisdiction is the first thing an organizer checks, not an afterthought. At the local level, petitions often go to a council or municipal body, with rules about residency, thresholds for debate or response, and formats that may be prescribed. At the regional level, petitions may go to a regional assembly or authority, with different thresholds, eligibility, and verification methods. At the national level, petitions may go to a legislature or government portal, with formal thresholds that trigger a debate, a response, or a committee review, and with strict rules about wording, eligibility, and verification. Beyond these levels, petitions to organizations, companies, and international bodies follow those bodies' own rules, which may be informal but still determine whether the petition is received and answered. The organizer's task is therefore comparative: to find the rules for their specific body, at their specific level, in their specific jurisdiction, and to design collection, validation, and submission around those rules.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part jurisdiction check. First, identify the decision-maker and its level precisely, because similar-sounding bodies at different levels have different rules. Second, obtain the body's current petition rules from its official source, and extract the threshold, eligibility, format, deadline, and response promise in plain words. Third, compare the rules across any levels the petition might target, and choose one target, because a petition designed for two levels at once usually satisfies neither. Fourth, design collection, validation, and submission around the chosen body's rules, and record the rules and their source in the petition's log, so any later question can be answered from the record. The demo below compares three example levels by threshold and response, which is the comparison organizers make before choosing a target.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Do not use it as a statement of the rules for any particular jurisdiction or body, because rules change and differ, and the body's current official rules govern. Do not use it to assume that a method valid in one jurisdiction is valid in another, because that assumption is the most common cross-jurisdiction error. title: Petition Timelines and Deadlines
body:
Petition timelines are unforgiving, because collection, validation, and submission each take time, and deadlines in formal petition systems are often strict. A realistic timeline works backwards from the submission deadline: it allows time for drafting and freezing the ask, for printing or building the collection form, for collection itself, for screening and deduplication, for assembling and copying the submission, and for the submission step, with a margin for the delays that always occur, such as a collector falling ill, a batch arriving late, or a form needing reprinting. Timelines also include the body's own timetable after submission: validation may take weeks, a response or debate may be scheduled months later, and the organizer should plan supporter communication for that waiting period, so supporters are not left wondering whether the petition vanished. A timeline written down, with owners and dates, is what separates a petition that arrives complete from one that arrives late, partial, or not at all.

Method. The working method for this record is a five-phase timeline plan. First, fix the submission deadline from the body's rules, and note how it is counted, including whether it falls on a working day. Second, work backwards, assigning dates to drafting, collection, screening, assembly, and submission, with a margin phase before submission for corrections. Third, assign an owner to each phase, so no phase waits for someone to claim it. Fourth, set check-ins during collection, at which the raw count, the estimated valid count, and the remaining time are reviewed together, so a shortfall is found early enough to fix. Fifth, plan post-submission communication: what supporters will be told, when, and by whom, during validation and while awaiting a response. The demo below lays out a small timeline in phases and counts them, which is the plan organizers write before their first collection day.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for petition timelines and deadlines. Do not use it as a guarantee that a timeline will hold, because collection rates vary and margins exist for that reason. Do not use it to compress screening or assembly to rescue a late collection, because a rushed submission is where errors that could have been caught become permanent. title: Responding to a Rejected Petition
body:
A rejected petition is a setback, not necessarily an ending, and how organizers respond determines whether the effort was wasted or merely delayed. Rejections happen for several distinct reasons, and each has a different remedy: a petition rejected for form, such as a missing field or wrong format, can often be corrected and resubmitted; a petition rejected for insufficient valid signatures can be re-run with better collection and a larger margin; a petition rejected because it addresses the wrong body can be redirected to the right one; a petition rejected because its ask falls outside the body's powers needs a redesigned ask; and a petition that was received but answered negatively has not been rejected at all, and its remedy is political, through further advocacy, not procedural. The first step in every case is the same: obtain the rejection reasons in writing, in full, and read them carefully, because organizers who guess at the reason often fix the wrong thing.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-step rejection response. First, obtain and record the rejection reasons in writing, with dates and the body's reference, and share them honestly with supporters. Second, classify the rejection: form, count, wrong body, out of powers, or negative answer, because each class has a different remedy. Third, choose the remedy that fits the class: correct and resubmit, re-run with better collection, redirect, redesign the ask, or continue advocacy, and do not resubmit an unchanged petition in the hope of a different result. Fourth, set a new timeline with the same discipline as the first attempt, including the margin and screening that prevent a repeat. The demo below classifies three example rejections by remedy, which is the classification organizers make before acting.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for responding to a rejected petition. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record after any petition rejection, and in civic education. Do not use it as legal advice about challenging a rejection, because appeal rights differ by jurisdiction and body, and organizers considering a challenge should seek qualified advice. Do not use it to resubmit an unchanged petition repeatedly, because repeated identical submissions waste the body's time and the petition's credibility. title: Petition Privacy and Signer Data
body:
Petition privacy matters because signers entrust organizers with personal data, such as names, addresses, and sometimes contact details, and that trust is part of what makes a petition legitimate. Organizers should collect only the data the rules require, state plainly to signers what will be collected, who will hold it, who will see it, and how long it will be kept, and honor that statement exactly. Paper forms should be stored securely, in a locked place with limited access, and never left in public or in vehicles; online data should be held under the platform's or body's terms as explained to signers, with access limited to those who need it for validation and submission. After submission, data should be handled as the rules and the organizer's statement require: some bodies retain petition data, some return or destroy it, and organizers must follow the applicable rule rather than improvising. Signers should never be contacted for unrelated purposes on the basis of a petition signature, and signer lists should never be shared, sold, or published beyond what the rules and the signers' consent allow.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-part privacy routine. First, minimize: collect only the fields the rules require, and no more. Second, state: tell signers, in plain words on the form, what is collected, who holds it, who sees it, and how long it is kept. Third, secure: store paper forms locked and online data access-limited, with a named holder responsible for them. Fourth, close: after submission, handle the data as the rules and the statement require, confirm that handling to signers where the statement promised it, and delete or return data that should not be retained. title: Petition Campaign Plan
body:
A petition campaign plan is the plan for the petition facet only: the ask, the target body, the collection method, the timeline, and the submission, kept separate from the wider organizing campaign, which is covered by the companion organizing basics database. The plan's value is focus: it prevents the petition from becoming a vague symbol of a cause and keeps it a countable, verifiable instrument aimed at one decision-maker. A good plan fits on two pages: the frozen ask, the target body and its rules, the eligibility conditions, the collection places and collectors, the timeline with its phases and owners, the screening and counting method, and the submission routine with its receipt step. The plan is written before collection, reviewed at each collection check-in, and kept as the petition's log, so any later question about the petition, from validators, decision-makers, or supporters, can be answered from it. Organizing around the petition, such as building a coalition or running public events, belongs to the organizing campaign, and this record deliberately does not duplicate it.

Method. The working method for this record is a six-part plan design. First, freeze the ask and record the target body and its rules, with their official source. Second, list the collection method, places, and collectors, with permissions confirmed. Third, write the timeline with phases, owners, and check-ins. Fourth, write the screening, deduplication, and counting method, with the three numbers it will produce. Fifth, write the submission routine, including the copy and receipt steps. Sixth, review the plan at each check-in, updating counts and dates but never changing the frozen ask without restarting collection under the new wording. The demo below lists a small plan's sections by status, which is the completeness check organizers run before their first collection day.

Do not use it as a substitute for the companion organizing basics database, which covers building support, coalitions, and campaigns around a cause.
